First reading: “They raised an objection: both a prostitute and a gentile woman.” It was first thought to mean a Jewish prostitute who is already a prostitute (e.g., she had relations with one liable for karet, or is promiscuous), so that payment to her is prohibited for anyone, even one permitted to her. That would be Rava’s view and refute Abaye, who derives “abomination,” “abomination” that payment applies only where betrothal does not take effect. The Gemara asks from the last clause, a widow with a High Priest, where betrothal does take effect, and answers that it is Rabbi Elazar, for whom an unmarried man with an unmarried woman renders her a prostitute, so every act outside full marriage is payment; the Rabbis would limit payment to relations where betrothal does not take effect. Tosafot asks how Abaye knows that Rabbi Elazar does not also derive “abomination,” “abomination,” and answers that since Rabbi Elazar is stricter about a prostitute than other tanna’im, he is stricter about payment too. On “Why specifically a widow?” and “since it is the paradigm,” Tosafot quotes Rashi (the unmarried case is the paradigm, so one might think a widow already forbidden to the High Priest is not payment) and calls it hard to understand; Rabbeinu Netanel explains that the paradigm equates payment with the priest’s prohibition of a prostitute, so a widow with a High Priest, forbidden under another name and not as a prostitute, might not be payment. Second reading (in the books, as printed here): the answer “It is Rabbi Akiva, who says betrothal does not take effect with those liable for prohibitions.” Tosafot asks why the Gemara adds “and this teaches us…,” and answers: had the baraita taught only the first clause, one might err and think that a woman who is already a prostitute counts as one for payment even when hired by a man permitted to her; the last clause teaches that payment arises only from relations where betrothal does not take effect, like a widow with a High Priest, according to Rabbi Akiva. Rava’s answer (“similar to a widow… until he says: This is for you”): Rashi says that for Rava a woman who was a prostitute from the outset has prohibited payment even without specification. Tosafot finds this forced, since according to the Rabbis there is no case where payment without specification is not payment, and proposes instead: payment given to a woman who already became a prostitute (through karet relations, or a promiscuous woman) by a man with whom betrothal takes effect is payment only if he states explicitly “Here is this lamb as your payment”; this excludes Rabbi Elazar, for whom it is payment even without specification. And “where she was a prostitute from the outset” means, also according to the Rabbis, where she becomes a prostitute through that very act for which he pays (e.g., his sister, or one liable for karet): then it is payment even without specification. Open on Sefaria for the full text.

messages.text: This is apparently a conclusive refutation of the opinion of Abaye.
In accordance with whose opinion is this baraita? It is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Akiva, who said: Betrothal does not take effect with regard to those liable for violating prohibitions.
messages.lead: The Gemara explains that Abaye could have said to you:
messages.quote: both a gentile prostitute and a Jewish prostitute, their payment is prohibited

messages.text: And this baraita teaches us that according to the opinion of Rabbi Akiva the halakha of payment to a prostitute applies to every prostitute with whom betrothal does not take effect, similar to the case of widow who is paid for engaging in intercourse with a High Priest, with whom betrothal does not take effect. This case is mentioned in the last clause of the baraita, cited below in the Gemara.

notes.he: להכי מדמו זונה ישר' לזונה עובדת כוכבים ומה זונה לא תפסי בה קידושי אף זונה ישראלית:
notes.en: Abaye could have said to you: that is why a Jewish prostitute is likened to a gentile prostitute: just as with a [gentile] prostitute betrothal does not take effect, so too the Jewish prostitute [of the baraita].

messages.text: And according to the opinion of Rava, what is different about the case specified in the continuation of the baraita, where it teaches: For example, a widow who is paid for engaging in intercourse with a High Priest? In Rava’s opinion even payment to an unmarried woman is considered payment to a prostitute.
messages.quote: so too payment to a Jewish prostitute is prohibited

messages.text: This teaches that even one who engaged in intercourse with an unmarried woman is similar in this regard to a widow who engages in intercourse with a High Priest: Just as in the case of a widow who engages in intercourse with a High Priest, they are flogged only if witnesses warned them that the act is prohibited and is punishable, so too with regard to one who engages in intercourse with a prostitute, it is not considered payment unless he says to her: This lamb is for you for services rendered, indicating that the intercourse is an act of prostitution.
The Gemara adds that this serves to exclude the opinion of Rabbi Elazar,
With regard to any unmarried man who engaged in intercourse with an unmarried woman not for the sake of marriage, he has thereby caused her to become a prostitute.

Rava, in contrast, holds that intercourse with an unmarried woman once does not render her a prostitute, unless he specifies that it is an act of prostitution by saying: This lamb is for services rendered. But Rava concedes that in a case where this woman was a prostitute from the outset, so too her payment is automatically prohibited even if she is unmarried.

The Gemara cites another version of Abaye’s answer to the objection from the baraita that teaches that payment to both a gentile prostitute and a Jewish prostitute is prohibited: When that baraita is taught, it is referring to those with whom relations are forbidden and with whom betrothal does not take effect. By contrast, when Abaye said that payment to a Jewish prostitute is not prohibited, he was referring to a case where betrothal does take effect.
messages.quote: both a gentile prostitute and a Jewish prostitute, their payment is prohibited

messages.text: But isn’t it taught in the last clause of the baraita: For example, a widow who is paid for engaging in intercourse with a High Priest, or a divorcée or a woman who has performed ḥalitza [ḥalutza] who is paid for engaging in intercourse with an ordinary priest, her payment is prohibited? But these are cases where betrothal takes effect.

notes.he: בעריות דלא תפסי בהו קידושי הא תפסי בהו קידושי אתנן מותר והא קתני סיפא דהאי ברייתא דאחד זונה עובדת כוכבים כו'. כגון אלמנה לכ"ג כו'. והנך תפסי בהו קידושי ואתננן אסור וקשיא לאביי:
notes.en: [It refers] to forbidden relations with whom betrothal does not take effect; but where betrothal takes effect, the payment is permitted. But the last clause of this baraita teaches: “Both a gentile prostitute, etc., for example, a widow with a High Priest, etc.” With these, betrothal takes effect and their payment is prohibited; this is difficult for Abaye.

messages.text: In accordance with whose opinion is this baraita?

notes.he: הא סיפא מני ר' אלעזר היא דאמר פנוי כו' שלא לשום אישות קידושין:
notes.en: Abaye could have said to you: this last clause, whose is it? It is Rabbi Elazar, who said: An unmarried man, etc., not for the sake of marriage [ishut], betrothal.

messages.text: Continues on 30a: it is in accordance with Rabbi Elazar, who says that an unmarried man who engages in intercourse with an unmarried woman not for the sake of marriage renders her a prostitute.
